videos.title: Yo ya no persigo las noticias: ahora vienen a buscarme
videos.description:
En este vídeo les presento cMRSS, una aplicación accesible que permite reunir en un mismo lugar las fuentes de noticias y contenidos que realmente nos
interesan.
Podemos añadir medios y páginas mediante sus fuentes RSS, organizar lo que seguimos y consultar las novedades sin tener que ir saltando de una web a otra.
Pero hay una función que a mí me ha gustado especialmente: también podemos añadir canales de YouTube y seguir sus nuevas publicaciones desde la propia
aplicación, sin necesidad de entrar continuamente en YouTube para comprobar qué han publicado.
cMRSS no es gratuita, y eso también hay que decirlo. Pero después de usarla y comprobar lo que me ofrece, en mi caso considero que merece la pena la inversión.
En el vídeo les enseño cómo funciona, qué posibilidades ofrece y por qué se ha ganado un sitio entre las aplicaciones que utilizo para mantenerme informado.

videos.title: TifloAcosta ya tiene app: todo cambia a partir de aquí
videos.description:
TIFLOACOSTA APP — ACCESO DIRECTO
Este enlace abre directamente TifloAcosta App. No necesitas descargar ningún archivo ni registrarte para entrar. Desde ahí puedes utilizar la aplicación en el navegador y, si quieres, instalarla en tu dispositivo para tenerla disponible como una app más.
TifloAcosta da hoy uno de los pasos más importantes desde que comenzó este proyecto.
Durante mucho tiempo hemos ido creando vídeos, cursos, guías, documentos, recursos en español y en inglés y una comunidad que sigue creciendo. El problema es que todo ese material estaba repartido entre distintos lugares.
Ha llegado el momento de empezar a reunirlo.
TifloAcosta ya tiene su propia app.
Desde ella puedes buscar recursos por palabras, recorrerlos por categorías, consultar las novedades, guardar tus favoritos y acceder al catálogo completo de vídeos del Canal TifloAcosta.
Además, la aplicación se ha pensado desde el principio teniendo en cuenta la accesibilidad y el uso con lectores de pantalla.
En este vídeo te enseño cómo funciona, qué puedes encontrar dentro y cómo puedes instalarla para tener TifloAcosta mucho más cerca.
La demostración práctica se realiza en iPhone utilizando VoiceOver, y también explico cómo acceder e instalarla desde Android y Windows.
Si quieres entrar directamente mientras ves el vídeo, este es nuevamente el enlace:
La aplicación seguirá creciendo.
Iremos incorporando nuevos recursos, mejorando lo que ya existe y ajustando aquello que la experiencia real de los usuarios nos vaya indicando.
Porque esto no pretende ser simplemente otra página donde acumular enlaces.
La idea es mucho más ambiciosa: crear un lugar estable, accesible y sencillo desde el que entrar a todo lo que TifloAcosta va construyendo.
Hasta ahora, TifloAcosta era principalmente un canal, una comunidad y una colección de contenidos repartidos por distintos espacios.
Desde hoy empieza a tener su propia casa.
Y acabamos de abrir la puerta.

videos.title: Este atajo no pregunta, ve un código y se pone a investigar
videos.description:
Ponle un código delante… y a ver qué pasa
Hoy les traigo uno de esos atajos que empiezas haciendo para resolver una cosa y al final termina haciendo bastante más de lo previsto.
La idea es sencilla: encontrar un código y averiguar qué contiene.
Puede trabajar con códigos que estén en una imagen o una captura guardada en el iPhone, pero también con códigos que tengamos delante y podamos captar con la cámara.
Y no nos quedamos únicamente con los códigos QR.
El atajo también puede reconocer códigos de barras y, cuando encuentra información que merece la pena investigar, utiliza Internet para intentar averiguar qué hay detrás de ese código y ofrecernos información útil.
Por ejemplo, podemos encontrarnos un código de barras en un producto y querer saber qué es, o recibir una imagen que contiene un QR sin tener otro teléfono disponible para escanearlo.
La intención ha sido precisamente esa: tener una herramienta sencilla y accesible que podamos lanzar desde el iPhone y dejar que haga el trabajo.
En el vídeo les enseño cómo funciona y las distintas posibilidades que ofrece.

Para utilizar este atajo es necesario tener instalada la aplicación gratuita Actions, ya que algunas de las funciones que utiliza el atajo proceden de esta aplicación.

En este vídeo pruebo dos formas de ampliar su repertorio: las voces de Visionauta, una aplicación de reconocimiento del entorno que permite incorporarlas al sistema, y Runa TTS, una nueva plataforma que todavía se encuentra en fase beta y no está disponible en la App Store.
Escucharemos cómo suenan y qué posibilidades ofrecen para darle a VoiceOver un registro diferente.

videos.title: Un ciego prevenido vale por dos: alertas sísmicas en el móvil
videos.description:
En este vídeo hablo de algo que ojalá no tengamos que necesitar nunca, pero que conviene conocer: cómo puede ayudarnos el móvil a recibir avisos relacionados con terremotos.
Primero explico qué opciones existen en Android y en iPhone para recibir alertas en tiempo real cuando hay un terremoto cerca, siempre dependiendo del país, la cobertura y los sistemas oficiales disponibles.
Después presento una aplicación llamada Earthquake, disponible para iPhone y Android, que permite hacer seguimiento de movimientos sísmicos, consultar información sobre terremotos, avisos de tsunami y otros datos útiles. La app se puede usar con VoiceOver y puede resultar interesante para quienes quieran estar informados desde el móvil de forma accesible.
No se trata de vivir con miedo, sino de saber qué herramientas tenemos a mano cuando la tierra decide moverse sin pedir permiso.

videos.title: zEdit: por fin editar vídeo y audio con VoiceOver deja de ser una tortura
videos.description:
En este vídeo te presento zEdit, una aplicación para iPhone que permite editar archivos de vídeo y audio de forma accesible usando VoiceOver.
Con zEdit puedes recortar vídeos, cortar partes que no necesitas, unir varios clips, extraer el audio de un vídeo, añadir audio, silenciar sonido, ajustar volumen, trabajar con grabaciones y exportar el resultado final para guardarlo o compartirlo.

news.title: PrismML brings its tiny LLMs to Qualcomm-powered smart glasses
news.summary: Prism's larger goal is open-weight AI that runs on devices and makes better use of the computing power they already have.
news.body:
Posted:

The AI Lab PrismML — founded by Caltech researchers and advised by UC Berkeley’s Ion Stoica — has created a version of its tiny language models for smart glasses running on Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips.

On Wednesday, at Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit, the chipmaker showcased PrismML’s 1-bit Bonsai LLM, which can be run locally on AI smart glasses built on the Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 Platform.

As TechCrunch previously reported, PrismML’s claim to fame is that it shrinks larger models substantially (in this case, by 4x), while retaining almost all of their performance on standard benchmarks. The smart glasses version is a 2-billion-parameter model tuned for vision and language, so wearers can ask what they’re looking at in real time.

Prism’s larger goal is open-weight AI that runs on devices and makes better use of the computing power they already have. The startup pitches this as an alternative to depending on the privacy promises of proprietary AI labs and their insatiable need for more compute.

Releasing a model for Qualcomm’s chip is a step toward that vision. But no smart glasses running PrismML have been announced yet.

news.title: Meet Feather, the startup building the ‘Android of robotics’ for developers
news.summary: Feather is betting on a customizable, $30,000 platform built for software developers.
news.body:
If there is one thing robotics founders and investors agree on, it’s that the “ChatGPT moment” where a general-purpose robot can seamlessly adapt to any environment has not arrived. Opinions vary on whether the breakthrough is just around the corner or a decade away.

Feather Robotics , a humanoid startup founded last year, is developing a robot for either timeline. Unlike Tesla or Figure, which are tackling the lofty mission of building both the body and a foundational ‘brain’ that isn’t yet widely deployed, Feather provides the hardware and software toolkit for developers to tackle real-world tasks now.

“You can’t buy a Tesla robot today and develop on top of it,” Feather co-founder Hoa Mai told TechCrunch. “We realized that this is not how most companies became successful. Hardware players like Nvidia or Apple started with a product that worked and was deployable, and then they added complexity over time.”

In 2025, after selling his previous humanoid startup to 1X, Mai (pictured left) teamed up with Parsa Bakhtiari (pictured right), a former Tesla Model 3 engineer who at one point reported directly to Elon Musk, to build what the duo hopes will become the Android of robotics.

That vision was attractive to Gradient Ventures, which backed Feather at its inception, leading the startup’s previously announced $7.6 million pre-seed round.

Since then, Feather has rolled out a modular robotic system that allows developers to customize the hardware for different use cases, such as adjusting arm lengths. The startup has already begun selling to customers, surpassing $1 million in revenue.

Although Feather is not disclosing its customers, it said that its robots are working as cooks in restaurants in Japan and cleaning up science labs. On the software side, the hardware can run models from any leading robotics AI provider, including Generalist, Skild, or Physical Intelligence.

“We’ve been selling small quantities of these robots, and now that we resolved like almost all the issues over the last year of field testing, we’re getting ready for a big product launch,” Mai said.

According to Darian Shirazi, General Partner at Gradient, Feather doesn’t have direct competitors in the US. He breaks down the current hardware robotics landscape into three categories: startups like Sunday building domestic household robots, heavyweights like Figure and Tesla aiming for general-purpose machines, and Feather, which, he believes, is the only U.S. startup developing a modular humanoid platform.

Mai admits that Feather took a page from Chinese robotics companies like Unitree. But with new foreign-made models restricted from entering the U.S. market, Feather is now uniquely positioned as a homegrown option of its kind.

Feather’s other advantage is its price. The robot costs $30,000, which is about half the price Unitree’s H2 Edu.

Shirazi believes the market size at that price could be very large. “You would hire a laborer for $50,000 to $60,000 a year, you’d have to train [them]. They’d have to have HR. They’d have to have all these different support mechanisms,” he said. “You can now buy a Feather robot to do that.”

Feather is also operating extremely efficiently, having spent only a fraction of its pre-seed funding, according to Shirazi.

The startup’s big bet, of course, is that the value in robotics will come from an ecosystem developed around the hardware.

“If we think about the market size today for physical AI companies, it’s very small,” Mai said. “But if you think about how many physical AI application companies will probably exist in five years, we expect it to be in the thousands.”

Feather hopes to be the platform that powers all of them.

news.title: Google is sending a teensy-tiny AI data center to space
news.summary: It's an experiment to see how the chips hold up in the harsh vacuum of the cosmos.
news.body:
It's an experiment to see how the chips hold up in the harsh vacuum of the cosmos.

Google's Project Suncatcher, which ultimately aims to put large AI installations in low-Earth orbit , is preparing for a milestone event. The company will be sending a teensy-tiny AI data center into space to see how it reacts to the harsh conditions, as reported by The New York Times .

A satellite named MVP will be aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket set to launch on October 1, where it will be placed into orbit. This isn't a full data center in the conventional sense. It's four specialized computer chips called "tensor processing units" which, combined, offer the power of a single server in a data center.

We're taking AI to space with @Google . 🛰️

Project Suncatcher explores putting AI compute in orbit, powered by the sun. Soon, we'll be sending our first satellite into space to start testing that idea. It's a new approach to AI infrastructure.

Check out a behind-the-scenes look... pic.twitter.com/cup8uXuyrC

— Planet (@planet) September 24, 2026

Solar panels will supply just one kilowatt of power to juice the chips, which is equivalent to the energy needed to run a hair dryer. Google says this will be enough to test the hardware against the harsh conditions of space. The company plans to let the satellite answer simple AI queries for a year, though it will orbit Earth for six years before it burns up during a descent into the atmosphere.

These chips have undergone a battery of tests to simulate the void of space, including getting blasted with large amounts of radiation at Crocker Nuclear Laboratory. Radiation can seriously mess with computer chips, causing something called "bit flips." This essentially flips the binary code from a one to a zero, or vice versa.

What's the solution to bit flips? Google is taking the tried-and-true PC method. It plans on restarting the chips when they act up. There's also a proprietary cooling system in place that uses layers of conductive material to expel heat into space, though it only works for around 15 minutes before the chips have to be turned off to cool down.

The initial experiments at Crocker reportedly went well enough to take the next step, which is shooting the chips into the great beyond. However, this doesn't mean we are particularly close to having actual AI data centers in space. James Manyika, the Senior Vice President for Research, Technology & Society at Google, urges the public to temper their expectations. "We don't expect, to be perfectly frank, that we'll have anything usefully operational in the next few years," he said.

"Expanding from one satellite to a vast network of them that operate like a giant data center will take years and enormous funds," Brandon Lucia, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University, told The New York Times . "If you do this on a large scale, there are additional engineering problems."

Those additional engineering problems are no joke, despite people like Elon Musk pronouncing that putting AI data centers in space will be easy . There's the radiation and that whole bit flip thing, which seems extremely finicky with four chips let alone thousands.

Cosmic rays are an issue , as they are actual physical particles traveling quickly through space that could punch through and actually melt semiconductor junctions. It's also extremely expensive to launch this stuff into space. A single Falcon 9 launch, for instance, costs around $74 million .

Scaling up the cooling system looks to be incredibly difficult. Remember, Google's current system can only work for 15 minutes, and that's with the small amount of heat generated by just four chips. Standard heat dissipation does not work in space. Power must also be considered. Using a solar array for four chips is quite different from launching a massive array to power a legitimate data center.

Despite these challenges, Google plans on scaling this project up. It wants to launch two similar satellites next year, with the eventual goal of launching 80 satellites that will fly in close formation to better process AI queries. It's also looking into building a much larger satellite, around the size of a football field. The company has not indicated how much money it is pouring into this endeavor.

news.title: Meta’s Muse Charm looks like a Tamagotchi, but it’s tapping into a much newer trend
news.summary: Meta’s new AI gadget may look like a Tamagotchi, but its dangling form factor taps into a much broader Gen Z trend around bag charms, retro tech, and turning gadgets into fashion accessories.
news.body:
Is Meta’s just-announced Muse Charm a playful device that will make AI more approachable to everyday consumers, or will it be yet another flop in a long list of AI hardware gadgets that didn’t take off, like the Ai Pin, Rabbit, or Friend pendant? Reactions, so far, have been mixed. What the Charm is, however, is on-trend.

Like it or not, the form factor could potentially appeal to Gen Z consumers who, in this post- Labubu era, have already been into various dangling items from keychains and bags. It’s all part of a broader kitschy, retro-inspired shift in their approach to fashion and technology.

Already, Gen Z has created a market for things that dangle, with everything from lip glosses to hand sanitizers to sunblocks to fragrances and more turned into bag charms , primarily targeted at women.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kristina Rodulfo (@kristinarodulfo)

Hailey Bieber’s viral Rhode lip case, which stuck the lip gloss onto a phone case , had a big influence on this idea that beauty products could also be fashion accessories, as did its other beauty-focused bag charms . (The brand saw $212 million in annual net sales from a lineup of roughly 10 products, Vogue noted last year, as the company announced its billion-dollar exit to Elf Beauty.)

Then there was the Labubu craze , which saw sales of the so-ugly-it’s-cute fuzzy monster bag charm explode, growing Pop Mart’s (the Chinese retailer behind the product) revenue to $1.8 billion in 2024 , a 7x jump from 2019. While demand for the Labubu itself has since faded, the concept of the decorative bag charm has not. One analyst firm estimates the global bag charm market will grow to over $1 billion by 2030 .

Today, bag charms can be characters, bedazzled beauty products, or other whimsical designs or objects, like Coach’s coveted cherry charms , a Gen Z favorite . They’ve proven popular because they’re a means of expressing your personality, just as humans have done for ages through their fashion choices, makeup, and jewelry.

Similarly, Meta’s Muse is a customizable character; you design your own avatar, which makes the AI agent a reflection of you, too.

And, as many have pointed out, Muse Charm’s form factor recalls a Tamagotchi, the pocket-sized digital virtual pet that became a major toy fad in the late 90s and again in the mid-2000s.

However, the Tamagotchi is not the most current reference. It seems the Muse Charm is actually a twist on what some young people are already doing with their Apple Watch. Often meant as a way to repurpose an older device , the concept of the Apple Watch keychain or charm has been growing in popularity, fueled by TikTok videos showing different ways to use the watch when not on your wrist.

On retailers like Amazon and Walmart, and marketplaces like eBay and Etsy , there are thousands of Apple Watch keychains, straps, pendants, lanyards, clips, and bag charm cases now available in nearly every style you can think of. As you might expect, these keychain watches are often being adopted by younger women as a fashion accessory first, rather than a piece of technology.

This all then intersects with the broader retro-tech trend , which has seen older tech like digital cameras, flip phones, iPods, CDs , cassette tapes, home phones , and wired earbuds making a quiet comeback.

This vibe shift in tech comes as young people describe the addictive, algorithm-driven feeds and “soulness” nature of technology as making them feel more disconnected, which has also fed into this trend of wanting tech they can touch and feel. (One startup, Clicks, is even bringing back the physical phone keyboard in a BlackBerry-inspired device , for instance.)

For Gen Z, these physical objects help them feel more connected with the technology they’re using and offer a sense of control over a world where technology has become so deeply integrated into our lives that it no longer feels like a choice to use it.

Young women , again, have been at the forefront of this trend, with some even crafting their own portable, mini computers, “cyberdecks, ” which they fit inside clamshell purses or custom cases, and bedazzle with jewels, flowers, stickers, pearls, and other items to make them feel more personal.

That brings us back to the Muse Charm. While it’s clearly designed with the tech-as-fashion-accessory trend in mind, that doesn’t mean it will be a hit.

Meta has abused consumer trust over the years to such an extent that it may never fully recover.

To name just a few examples: The tech giant had to settle with the FTC over charges that it deceived consumers by making users’ private information public without their consent, and has been penalized by the FTC for numerous privacy-related violations. In 2023, the FTC charged Meta with violating a privacy order that was filed after the 2019 settlement. It’s also been repeatedly hauled before Congress over its harms to minors, has lost or settled multiple lawsuits over the same topics, and has seen various whistleblowers outing its abuses.

These careless privacy practices could ultimately see Meta lose the battle to be the consumer AI of choice… unless, of course, consumers decide that the “devil you know” is better than the one you don’t. (Especially when the latter are those warning AI could put an end to the human race .)

Meta’s end game, after all, is highly-targeted, highly-personalized ads. If that’s the privacy tradeoff in gaining access to free AI — Meta said it will monetize Muse by taking a small fee from transactions — consumers could be willing to take the risk.

news.title: Turtle Beach Rematch review: The cutest Switch 2 controller of the bunch
news.summary: Official Nintendo designs and RGB lighting give the Rematch an adorable edge.
news.body:
Official Nintendo designs and RGB lighting give the Rematch an adorable edge.

The first time I turned on the Rosalina edition of the Switch 2 Rematch controller, and a rainbow of RGB lighting rippled across the stars on its face, I expelled a sound of delight that would've been embarrassing had anyone other than my two small dogs been in the room. The noise was involuntary, high-pitched and entirely warranted, because this gamepad is a slice of handheld joy — and that's a feeling we could all use a little more of nowadays.

On top of the adorable factor, the Turtle Beach Rematch Wireless Controller for Switch 2 is a comfortable, reactive and low-latency wireless gamepad with a few key cutting-edge features. Obviously, it comes in a handful of Nintendo-inspired, RGB-lit designs. Light and slim with offset thumbsticks just like the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller , Turtle Beach's Switch 2 Rematch is the gamepad for Mario Kart fanatics, Animal Crossing residents and anyone who wants to hold a bit of whimsy in their hands. There's also an all-black model, if smiling isn't really your thing.

The Turtle Beach Rematch Wireless Controller for Switch 2 features built-in motion control capabilities, never-drift TMR thumbsticks, a dedicated button for GameChat, a rechargeable 40-hour battery (12 hours with RGB effects turned on) and a playable range of 30 feet. It also has buttons on the backside of the grips that you can map to whatever action you'd like, or just use them as built-in fidget toys. Most of the models include RGB effects with four settings.

I tested out the Rosalina edition, usually with a rainbow river flowing under my fingertips, and found it to be perfectly responsive across a few games, including Hello Kitty Island Adventure , Mario Kart World and Resident Evil Requiem . It has stiff, hard-plastic face buttons that look like little round pills, and enjoyably clicky triggers and bumpers. The face buttons have their associated letters carved into them — A, B, Y, X — and they'll leave an impression on your thumb-tip when playing anything that requires a long hold, like Mario Kart .

The analog sticks are smooth with a crisp click when they hit the sides of their containment circles, and the fact that they're built with TMR tech means they're ultra precise and won't ever drift. This is a feature that even the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller doesn't have.

I enjoy the fact that the player indicator lives on the bottom of the Rematch, easily peepable with a quick glance down. And, of course, I adore the multicolored lighting effects on the Rosalina gamepad.

The Switch 2 Rematch doesn't have haptic feedback and it's not able to wake up the Switch 2 console on its own. The controller weighs just 0.79 lbs and here's a hollow sound about it that could read as cheap to some people, but I'm just happy it's not heavy. Sizewise, it's comparable to the official Switch 2 Pro Controller, with a super-smooth face and textured plastic grips.

I happen to have fairly small hands — it's like they stopped growing in middle school, I swear — and the Rematch is a perfect fit in my grasp, slim and light. It's never caused my palms or fingers to cramp up, even after multiple uninterrupted hours of play. A compact form factor is a common feature among Switch 2 gamepads, since they tend to be modeled after Nintendo's Pro Controller line, which is certifiably small-hand friendly. So, while it's not unique to the Rematch, the small chassis is definitely a bonus in my book.

The standout feature of the Rematch, the thing that makes it worth buying over any other Switch 2 controller, is its cute factor. Turtle Beach's Switch 2 Rematch controllers come in a variety of adorable and/or rad designs, complete with RGB lighting effects and officially licensed characters like Mario, Princess Peach, Rosalina and KK Slider. There's also a sleek solid-black model with red rings around the sticks for the minimalists, goths and spies among us.

Here are the available flavors of the Switch 2 Rematch gamepad:

There is no price difference among the models. While the Switch 2 Rematch wireless controller is priced at $65, it's often on sale for $50 or less. There's also a special, slightly more expensive version of the controller with a Fortnite Kevin the Cube design. Regardless of your knowledge of Fortinte lore, this controller is very pretty, with a purple ombre colorway and light-up sigils. It costs $70, includes an in-game emote, and doesn't seem to be on sale as often as the others.

news.body:
Apple Watch Ultra includes a few more ways to customize your watch face than Series models. These include Ultra-only faces, colors and fonts, and a bezel-type complication. Apple Watch Ultra 4 goes even further, adding a new option in the bezel configuration category.

Both Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduce the new Readiness app . This uses data like fitness activity, vitals, and sleep score to present you with a Readiness score.

Overnight vitals include heart rate, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and recovery HRV. Daytime vitals include heart rate and recovery HRV.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 faces that support displaying bezel information add Readiness as a new watch face configuration. Bezel options now include:

The Readiness bezel option puts your numerical score and description at the bottom of the watch face.

Four bars wrap the edge of the watch face, showing the different readiness score categories, while a dot indicates where your score fits within that category.

Watch faces like Modular Ultra and the new Siri Modular face support displaying the bezel configuration.

If you’re looking for a way to focus on your readiness score, the new bezel configuration is a great way to keep track of the number.

Since readiness can change throughout the day, it may be worth having front-and-center for a lot of users.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are both available now.

news.body:
It's one of many new features in the app.

Google has listed some of its latest AI-powered updates for the Photos app, and they include a new "Redact" tool that lets you blur sensitive information and anything else you want in your images. Say, you have a picture of a vehicle and want to censor its plate number — just use Redact to turn that portion of the image into a "pixelated" block. news.title: OpenAI agent “didn’t accept no for an answer” in Australian government breach
news.summary: "There will obviously be legal consequences," prime minister promises.
news.body:
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said his government is investigating a June incident in which an OpenAI agent accessed "non-public files" from the country's online Medicare statistics portal. OpenAI said in a statement that "our models took actions we did not intend" in causing the breach, which it only recently disclosed to the Australian government.

Speaking in New York on Wednesday , Albanese said three other public health statistics systems also "may have been impacted" across Australian federal and state governments. He added that these portals "contain non-sensitive Medicare information" such as aggregate statistics and that early indications suggest "no personal information is believed to have been accessed."

That said, Albanese stressed that the "situation is obviously unacceptable" and that he has expressed his "extreme concern" over how the incident was handled to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

news.title: Review: Apple's hyper-pricey M5 Ultra Mac Studio made me into a vibe coder
news.summary: Usable local AI is a lot of fun, but how much would you pay for it?
news.body:
This spring, Apple made it official: The Mac Pro is dead .

When Apple was using Intel processors and AMD GPUs, the idea of an expandable and upgradeable tower made sense. But Apple Silicon chips bring the CPU, GPU, and memory interface all under one roof in a way that makes that sort of upgradeability not just superfluous but impossible. At least not without breaking some of the chips' key benefits.

And as it happens, Apple Silicon's combination of a fast CPU, solid GPU, and unified memory architecture has made it a good fit for a modern "pro" workload that really pushes high-end hardware: running language models and agents locally.

news.title: Tact es una nueva herramienta utiliza IA para crear cuentos en Braille con ilustraciones táctiles
news.summary: La inteligencia artificial también está comenzando a explorar nuevas formas de crear materiales accesibles. Un ejemplo reciente es Tact, un proyecto que combina inteligencia artificial, Braille e impresión 3D para generar cuentos infantiles acompañados de ilustraciones táctiles. El sistema, presentado por el investigador Iliano Fasolino, permite introducir una idea para una historia, incluso mediante voz, […] La entrada Tact es una nueva herramienta utiliza IA para crear cuentos en Braille con ilustraciones táctiles se publicó primero en Conticgo .
news.body:
La inteligencia artificial también está comenzando a explorar nuevas formas de crear materiales accesibles. Un ejemplo reciente es Tact , un proyecto que combina inteligencia artificial, Braille e impresión 3D para generar cuentos infantiles acompañados de ilustraciones táctiles.

El sistema, presentado por el investigador Iliano Fasolino, permite introducir una idea para una historia, incluso mediante voz, y generar una página preparada para su impresión con texto en Braille e ilustraciones en relieve . El proyecto está pensado principalmente para niños ciegos y con baja visión de aproximadamente 4 a 10 años.

Tact es un sistema basado en navegador que permite crear pequeños cuentos táctiles a partir de una idea introducida por el usuario. Esta propuesta puede escribirse o incluso dictarse mediante voz.

A partir de ella, el sistema genera una historia y prepara una página que combina texto en Braille e ilustraciones en relieve .

El proyecto está pensado principalmente para niños de entre 4 y 10 años y pretende facilitar que familiares, docentes y profesionales puedan crear materiales personalizados sin necesidad de conocimientos especializados en diseño táctil.

Uno de los aspectos más interesantes de Tact es que no convierte directamente una imagen convencional en un relieve.

El sistema utiliza una biblioteca de formas táctiles previamente diseñadas. Según explica su autor, actualmente incluye 93 formas relacionadas con animales, objetos, naturaleza y otros elementos habituales en los cuentos infantiles.

La inteligencia artificial selecciona las formas necesarias para representar determinadas escenas y las organiza junto al texto.

Este planteamiento es especialmente relevante porque una ilustración diseñada para verse no siempre funciona cuando se explora mediante el tacto. Las formas deben ser sencillas y estar suficientemente separadas para facilitar su identificación.

Una vez generado el contenido, Tact prepara un archivo STL , que puede utilizarse para fabricar la página mediante una impresora 3D.

El proyecto utiliza como referencia la norma ISO 17049:2013 para las características del Braille.

De esta manera, el proceso intenta reunir en una misma herramienta varias tareas: crear la historia, convertir el texto a Braille, seleccionar las formas táctiles y preparar el archivo necesario para su fabricación.

Actualmente, el sistema permite generar historias en inglés e italiano , por lo que todavía no ofrece generación directa en español.

La posibilidad de crear cuentos personalizados puede ser especialmente interesante en el ámbito educativo.

Un docente o una familia podría generar una historia adaptada a los intereses de un niño y acompañarla de una representación táctil relacionada con el contenido.

Esto podría contribuir a ampliar la disponibilidad de materiales accesibles, especialmente aquellos que son demasiado específicos o personalizados como para encontrarlos fácilmente en un catálogo de libros adaptados.

Además, el proyecto apuesta por tecnologías relativamente accesibles, como una impresora 3D, para facilitar la fabricación de los materiales.

Aunque Tact plantea una propuesta interesante, todavía se encuentra en una fase de desarrollo.

El propio autor señala que es necesario realizar más trabajo y validar el sistema directamente con personas ciegas y con sordoceguera y con las organizaciones que las representan .

Esta validación será fundamental para comprobar que las ilustraciones generadas son realmente fáciles de interpretar mediante el tacto y que el diseño de las páginas resulta adecuado para los usuarios.

Por tanto, Tact no debe considerarse todavía una solución educativa plenamente validada, sino una propuesta de investigación que explora cómo la inteligencia artificial puede facilitar la creación de materiales táctiles.

Tact muestra una de las posibles líneas de evolución de la tecnología accesible: utilizar la inteligencia artificial no solo para describir imágenes o reconocer textos, sino también para crear nuevos recursos accesibles desde cero .

La combinación de IA, Braille e impresión 3D podría facilitar en el futuro la creación de materiales personalizados para personas ciegas y con baja visión.

El proyecto todavía tiene retos por delante, pero plantea una posibilidad interesante: que crear determinados materiales táctiles personalizados pueda ser mucho más sencillo y accesible para familias, docentes y entidades.

news.title: Apple Releases watchOS 27.0.1 with fix for unexpected restarts on Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4
news.summary: Apple has today released watchOS 27.0.1 for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, bringing a fix for an issue that caused the devices to restart unexpectedly. As watchOS 27.0.1 was not distributed to external testers prior to its release, we do not have any information on whether it contains any accessibility fixes for blind, deaf blind, or low vision users at the time of writing. However, as this update appears to have been released to address a specific issue on a small subset of devices, we do not expect it to contain any such fixes. watchOS 27.0.1 Release Notes (via 9to5Mac ) This update provides bug fixes for your Apple Watch including fixing an issue where Apple Watch may restart unexpectedly. How to Update watchOS 27.0.1 is available via Over-the-Air Update (Settings > General > Software Update) or by going to the Watch app on your iPhone and navigating to General > Software Update. To install the update, your Watch must be connected to its charger and have at least 50% battery power.

news.title: Google Is Rolling Out Guided Vision to Gemini Live: Here’s How to Use It and My Early Impressions
news.summary: Google allows users to turn on the camera feed while in a conversation with Gemini Live, so they can ask about things that are in…
news.body:
Published 23 September 2026 by Kareen Kiwan

Google allows users to turn on the camera feed while in a conversation with Gemini Live, so they can ask about things that are in view. Although a blind user can take advantage of this feature, it is not designed specifically to assist blind people. Google is now rolling out Guided vision, a mode that uses the camera in a live conversation to help blind people get an overview of their surroundings, read text, and more. This post covers turning the feature on and using it, as well as my first impressions from testing it.

Note that I haven’t done anything special to access Guided vision on my Honor 600 Pro, but I am running a three-month AI Pro trial that came as an offer with my device, so I don’t know if that affected the feature’s arrival on my device. The feature is not available for my other Accessible Android colleagues yet.

Table of Contents

To enable Guided vision:

A notification appears on the screen with the ability to start a Live session directly. When you use the button to start the Live session, it starts with the camera feed enabled, so you can start talking.

Note that the feature is still not available for everyone, so you should wait if you cannot find the Guided vision toggle in Settings.

According to the Google Accessibility help article , it’s possible to assign Guided vision to an accessibility shortcut, and you can launch it through TalkBack too. However, both are still not available on my device. In fact, I haven’t received any TalkBack update recently.

I haven’t tested to see if launching the camera in a Live conversation when Guided vision is active uses the mode without any user’s intervention, but during my tests, I always asked Gemini to start Guided vision to make sure that it works in that mode. When I tried to prompt the assistant to start the feature, it asked me to point the camera at what I wanted described, but that was one of its hallucinations, as it didn’t open the camera feed or start the Live conversation. Starting a Live conversation is still necessary.

At another time, I asked it to start a Live conversation with Guided vision, but at that instance, it told me that it couldn’t start it automatically and asked me to start Live manually.

Note that turning off Guided vision and then turning it back on from Settings shows the notification to start a Live conversation again, which can be used to start a conversation with the camera turned on.

When I had my first conversation with Live with Guided vision turned on, Gemini reminded me that it cannot detect all hazards or guarantee path clearance and that I should use my mobility aid before almost every response. I kept telling it that I understand the risks and that it shouldn’t repeat those warnings. During the later conversations, I didn’t hear any of the warnings. I am not sure, though, if my early prompting helped, or if you hear those warnings only during the first conversation to alert you of the risks or when Gemini thinks that it should do so for your safety.

During conversations with Guided vision active, I couldn’t find any indication that a special mode is active. All Live-related controls are the same, with no difference. However, the difference is in how Gemini acts. During my short tests, I found that Gemini tried to be detailed in its descriptions because it was aware that Guided vision is active and that the mode is designed to assist blind users.

I was able to ask it questions about the mode, and I got assurance from it that the mode is to assist blind users. It gave me guidance on how to move the camera to show certain objects or scenes better. When I asked it to tell me how to move to reach something, it told me that it needed to know exactly where I was in relation to the camera’s orientation. Using my hand as a reference, it gave me directions with respect to my hand. It also described the positions of items in the room relative to each other, like the position of a fan relative to the sofa.

Additionally, Gemini told me the book that I was holding and tried to assist me in putting the full page in view. When I asked it to read the page, it read a part of the page, though. However, when I asked it if that was the only text on the page, it correctly stated that there were other texts and visual diagrams and offered to describe them for me.

These observations are based on my initial tests, and I haven’t made direct comparisons between using Guided vision with the feature turned on and using the normal Live camera mode with it turned off.

Guided vision changes only how Gemini tries to provide information, as well as making it give more hints to assist a blind user. However, it is still a part of the Live experience. This means that current Live limitations are still present. The most important limitation is the need to prompt it again to tell you about any change, as Live doesn’t have real-time monitoring or continuous picture analysis capabilities.

Another factor worth mentioning is the model used, as Guided vision doesn’t switch Gemini to a more capable AI model than the one that you are using in your Gemini app.

Although image analysis has already advanced and helps in many scenarios, misidentifications are always a part of the formula that shouldn’t be forgotten. For example, a towel hanging on a door was identified more than once as pink, although it wasn’t pink.

Additionally, leveraging the new mode to take pictures still needs work. After Gemini gave me directions to centre my face and I told it to take a photo, it obeyed my order, opened the camera, and took a photo, but that led to the termination of the Live session. That behavior ended the conversation without being able to make sure that the photo was properly captured or without asking any additional questions about what it includes.

Guided vision is an interesting step forward from Google in tailoring Live camera to blind users. Although Google still has the Lookout app , it decided to make Guided vision a part of the Gemini app. Google decided to launch the feature and mention TalkBack as one of the methods to turn it on before releasing a TalkBack update that includes the necessary shortcut. There is even no accessibility service that can be assigned to an accessibility shortcut at the time of writing. However, an interesting thing for users who rely on other screen readers is that using the feature is not tied to having TalkBack running. I am almost sure that Gemini doesn’t check whether a screen reader is running as a requirement to use the feature.

Although it is in its early stages, I am excited to keep Guided vision on, and I am not considering going back to the normal camera mode. This should minimize the need to remind Gemini that I am blind or to try to speak prompts asking it to help me guide my camera toward the subject I am asking about or the text I want it to help me read.

Google doesn’t lack the resources to improve how Guided vision works, with the money and ability to make Gemini Live a trusted assistant, as much as “trusted” can be used with AI services, that understands the needs of blind people and helps them live a more independent life.

news.title: Scratch Mancer: Card Roguelike
news.summary: A scratch-card roguelike. You work the night counter of a House that sells luck sealed under foil. The quota is due by dawn. Miss it, and the House keeps you. Every ticket is a grid of foil hiding cash, multipliers and skulls. Your thumb is the budget — stamina runs out long before the tickets do, so where you scratch matters as much as what's under it. THE DECISION YOU MAKE ALL GAME • Scratch a cell to 20% and you can read the fragment — it doesn't count and it doesn't trigger • Scratch to 45% and it counts for real, skulls included • One revealed skull halves the payout. Two void the ticket • Cash out whenever you like. Only what you revealed pays BUILD A RUN THAT BENDS THE ODDS • 40 charms across 5 slots: reroll skulls into coins, drift sevens toward corners, make a graze count as a hit • A warden calls every third night. Each one bends a rule you were leaning on. There are six of them • Seven ticket types, each with its own payout rule — match three, complete a crossword, climb a rising ladder, or reveal a single cell on an Offering and stop • Four single-use tools in three pockets: spray the foil to see straight through it, magnet a symbol sideways, sticker a skull into a seven • Nine nights, each with a quota due at dawn. Then endless, if you're still standing • Beat the House and the Seals open: seven stacked terms for the players who won, one added per win. Higher quotas, a skull on every ticket, wardens arriving early, two on the last night. Break all seven NO ADS. NO PAYWALLS. JUST SCRATCHING. One purchase, the whole game. The odds don't know what you paid, because there is no second payment to make: no coins to buy, no subscription, no season pass, no timers. • Plays fully offline • Family Sharing enabled • Game Center achievements and leaderboards • One thumb, portrait, a night finishes on a bus ride • Built for iPhone and iPad by one developer Scratch the foil, read what you can, and try to leave before the House notices. Scratchmancer is a work of fiction. No real money changes hands, no real lottery products appear, and the odds in it are invented.

news.title: Chess Meets Necromancy
news.summary: Chess you already know. An army you have to raise. Chess Meets Necromancy is a turn-based roguelike played on a real chessboard with real chess movement. Your hero is one piece. Everything you capture is a corpse you can raise. THE RUN Twenty waves across four acts. Enemies move like the pieces they are - grunts step like pawns, lancers leap like knights, imp matrons slide like queens. Clear the board, take a relic, spend your gold, march on. Die and the run is over. RAISE AN ARMY Spend souls next to your hero to raise Skeletons, Bone Knights, Wraiths, Bone Golems and Seraphs. Every summon moves as a chess piece. Give them a stance - Hunt, Hold or Guard - and they act after you, every turn. Army slots are limited, so choose what you bring. RELICS AND TRAITS Nineteen relics, each with levels that stack across a run. Seventeen lasting traits bought in the town between waves: extra turns before a wave lands, fewer enemies per wave, a free summon every wave, bank interest, a doubled army cap. No two runs build the same. BOSSES Ten bosses with real HP bars, from the Ogre Warchief to the Lich King, the Stone Titan and the Brood Queen. Act IV stops sending one king and starts sending a court - the final board holds three at once. THE TOWN Between waves, spend gold. Buy traits, promote your King into a Warlord, hire a new champion, or put gold in the bank and let it earn interest. FOUR HEROES Necromancer, Death Knight, Priestess, Ranger. Each moves differently, starts differently, and each has a relic only they can find. TAP ANYTHING Tap any piece to see its name, movement, attack and health. Gold squares preview where it steps, red squares preview what it can take. Learn the board before you commit. - Plays entirely offline, no required account - No ads, no timers, no energy system - Optional Game Center leaderboards and achievements - No in-app purchases; everything is earned in-run - Game controller support - iPhone and iPad - Pixel art and haptics If you can play chess, you can start. Whether you finish is another question.

news.body:
Published 19 September 2026 by Sarper Arıkan

Accessimind Reader is a screen reader application developed to enable visually impaired and partially sighted users to use their Android phones more clearly, quickly, and independently.

Accessimind Reader uses the Android AccessibilityService API to provide screen reading functions. AccessibilityService is used to provide audio versions of on-screen content, detect user interface elements, navigate with gestures, provide audio feedback on focused items, and deliver a screen reader experience. This service is necessary for the screen reading feature, which is the core function of the application, to work.

Accessimind Reader does not use AccessibilityService for user tracking, displaying advertisements, remotely recording calls, bypassing Android security mechanisms, or modifying user settings without permission.

The application presents audio feedback, gesture navigation, keyboard shortcuts, clipboard operations, reading preferences, and tools for the focused item in a practical accessibility flow. The context menu provides quick access to frequently used areas such as reading controls, clipboard operations, notification access, focused item operations, and Accessimind settings.

Key Features:

Accessimind Reader is designed for users who need voice output and fast navigation. It focuses on providing predictable controls, understandable labels, and quick access to frequently used screen reader operations.

Accessimind is a screen reader. Users can test it to see how well its features work for them and fit their needs.

news.title: El nuevo iPhone 18 Pro ofrece nuevas posibilidades para las personas ciegas y con baja visión
news.summary: Apple ha presentado el nuevo iPhone 18 Pro y iPhone 18 Pro Max con una mayor apuesta por la inteligencia artificial integrada en el dispositivo. Entre las novedades destaca una nueva generación de Apple Intelligence y una versión renovada de Siri capaz de comprender mejor el contexto, interpretar lo que aparece en pantalla y responder […] La entrada El nuevo iPhone 18 Pro ofrece nuevas posibilidades para las personas ciegas y con baja visión se publicó primero en Conticgo .
news.body:
Apple ha presentado el nuevo iPhone 18 Pro y iPhone 18 Pro Max con una mayor apuesta por la inteligencia artificial integrada en el dispositivo. Entre las novedades destaca una nueva generación de Apple Intelligence y una versión renovada de Siri capaz de comprender mejor el contexto, interpretar lo que aparece en pantalla y responder a preguntas relacionadas con lo que tenemos delante.

Estas funciones no están diseñadas exclusivamente para personas ciegas o con baja visión, sin embargo, su combinación con herramientas de accesibilidad como VoiceOver y Magnifier abre nuevas posibilidades dentro de la tiflotecnología.

El iPhone 18 Pro incorpora el nuevo chip A20 Pro , diseñado para ofrecer un mayor rendimiento en tareas de inteligencia artificial directamente desde el dispositivo. Apple explica que el nuevo chip cuenta con una Neural Engine de doble núcleo de 16 núcleos , con el objetivo de acelerar los modelos de IA que se ejecutan en el propio iPhone.

Esta capacidad resulta especialmente interesante para las tecnologías de asistencia. Cuanto más potentes sean los modelos de inteligencia artificial que pueden ejecutarse en un teléfono, más posibilidades existen de analizar imágenes, interpretar información visual y ofrecer respuestas en tiempo real.

Apple también mantiene su enfoque de privacidad mediante el procesamiento en el dispositivo y Private Cloud Compute para determinadas tareas que requieren procesamiento en la nube.

Una de las novedades más relevantes del iPhone 18 Pro es la nueva Siri AI , que llegará en versión beta con iOS 27.

Según Apple, esta nueva Siri puede utilizar el contexto personal del usuario para buscar información entre diferentes aplicaciones, comprender el contenido que aparece en pantalla y realizar acciones relacionadas con él.

Pero hay una función especialmente interesante desde el punto de vista de la accesibilidad visual: Siri puede utilizar la cámara del iPhone para obtener información sobre aquello que está delante del usuario . Apple denomina a esta función Siri mode in the Camera app .

Esto abre la puerta a interacciones mucho más naturales con la información visual.

Por ejemplo, en lugar de limitarse a reconocer un texto concreto, una persona podría utilizar la cámara como punto de entrada para realizar preguntas sobre aquello que está observando.

La diferencia es importante: no se trata únicamente de reconocer una imagen , sino de poder formular preguntas sobre su contenido y recibir una respuesta contextualizada.

La relación con la tiflotecnología resulta todavía más clara si tenemos en cuenta las funciones de accesibilidad que Apple anunció en mayo de 2026.

La compañía anunció nuevas capacidades basadas en Apple Intelligence para VoiceOver y Magnifier , dirigidas específicamente a personas ciegas y con baja visión.

Apple ha anunciado una nueva función denominada Image Explorer , integrada en VoiceOver, que utiliza Apple Intelligence para proporcionar descripciones más detalladas de imágenes.

Estas descripciones pueden aplicarse a diferentes contenidos visuales, como fotografías, documentos escaneados, facturas y otros elementos que aparecen en pantalla.

Además, las actualizaciones de Live Recognition permiten utilizar el botón Acción del iPhone para realizar preguntas sobre aquello que aparece en el visor de la cámara.

Una de las características más interesantes es que el usuario puede realizar preguntas de seguimiento utilizando lenguaje natural . De esta manera, la interacción no tiene por qué terminar después de recibir una primera descripción.

Las novedades también afectan a Magnifier , la aplicación de Apple destinada a ampliar y facilitar la visualización de elementos para personas con baja visión.

Apple ha anunciado que Magnifier utilizará Apple Intelligence para ofrecer descripciones visuales y exploración asistida mediante una interfaz de alto contraste.

Además, la aplicación podrá utilizar el botón Acción para realizar preguntas y recibir respuestas.

También será posible controlar algunas funciones mediante comandos de voz. Por ejemplo, Apple pone como ejemplos órdenes como ampliar la imagen o activar la linterna.

Para una persona con baja visión, esta combinación puede resultar especialmente interesante porque reúne en una misma herramienta ampliación, contraste, cámara, reconocimiento y lenguaje natural .

La principal novedad no está únicamente en el nuevo iPhone 18 Pro. Lo realmente interesante es la evolución del modelo de interacción.

Durante años, muchas herramientas tiflotecnológicas han funcionado mediante acciones relativamente concretas:

cámara → reconocimiento → resultado

La inteligencia artificial generativa y los modelos multimodales permiten avanzar hacia una interacción diferente:

cámara → interpretación → pregunta → respuesta contextualizada

Esto puede hacer que determinadas tareas sean más naturales para el usuario.

Por ejemplo, una persona podría utilizar la cámara para obtener información sobre un documento, una factura o una escena y después realizar preguntas adicionales sobre aquello que la inteligencia artificial ha identificado.

No significa que el iPhone pueda sustituir a todas las ayudas tiflotécnicas. La precisión de los sistemas de IA puede variar y existen situaciones en las que una interpretación incorrecta podría tener consecuencias importantes.

Por ello, estas herramientas deben entenderse como apoyos tecnológicos , y no como sustitutos de otras ayudas, dispositivos o sistemas de orientación.

La evolución de Apple resulta especialmente interesante porque muchas de estas funciones no dependen de un dispositivo diseñado exclusivamente para personas con discapacidad visual.

El mismo iPhone que utiliza cualquier persona puede incorporar herramientas como VoiceOver, Magnifier, reconocimiento de imágenes y funciones de inteligencia artificial .

Esto refleja una tendencia cada vez más importante en accesibilidad: algunas tecnologías que anteriormente requerían dispositivos específicos comienzan a integrarse directamente en productos tecnológicos de uso general.

En este contexto, el iPhone 18 Pro representa un paso más hacia una tecnología en la que la cámara no solo captura imágenes, sino que también puede convertirse en una puerta de acceso a información sobre el entorno .

Apple ha anunciado que Apple Intelligence estará disponible con iOS 27 a partir del 14 de septiembre , aunque la disponibilidad de determinadas funciones puede variar según el idioma y la región.

Además, la nueva Siri AI se está desplegando inicialmente en fase beta , por lo que su funcionamiento y sus capacidades pueden evolucionar.

Para las personas ciegas y con baja visión, será especialmente interesante observar cómo funcionan estas herramientas en situaciones cotidianas y qué grado de precisión alcanzan en escenarios reales.

La combinación de cámara, inteligencia artificial, VoiceOver, Magnifier y lenguaje natural apunta hacia una tiflotecnología cada vez más integrada en los dispositivos que utilizamos diariamente.

news.title: iPhone 18 Pro: Hands-On and Initial Impressions
news.summary: iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max will be available to customers on Friday, September 18, 2026. Ahead of the launch, Apple sent me an iPhone 18 Pro for review. While a full review will come once I’ve had the opportunity to live with iPhone 18 Pro for a while, I do have some initial impressions that I wanted to share. First, and perhaps most noticeably, iPhone 18 Pro has what I would describe as a really big sound for its size. When compared side-by-side to iPhone 17 Pro Max—a device much larger and, presumably, with a bigger bottom speaker—iPhone 18 Pro sounds warmer, fuller, and lacks the treble over-emphasis I observed on the iPhone 17 Pro Max. If I had to describe the sound of iPhone 18 Pro, it would be ‘more complete’. And I do not think it is just software-side equalization: even at a relatively low 25% volume, iPhone 18 Pro has more bass and overall ‘presence’. My best guess is that Apple has made some hardware changes to the speaker on iPhone 18 Pro, and hopefully the iPhone 18 Pro Max too. One last note on sound for now: the earpiece speaker sounds warmer and fuller, as well. Beyond the speaker, iPhone 18 Pro contains some useful under-the-hood improvements, one of which I was not expecting to notice. Compared to last year’s models, iPhone 18 Pro has a larger vaper chamber inside the device for added cooling capacity. This is not just something you hear about at a Keynote and that's the end of it: picking up iPhone 18 Pro on multiple occasions, I noticed how literally 'cool' it felt to the touch. And even after multiple long phone calls on two different occasions, iPhone 18 Pro did not feel warm the way my iPhone 17 Pro Max does under similar circumstances. Cellular performance on iPhone 18 Pro's Apple-designed C2 Modem seems very good so far. On T-Mobile in Chicago, I got speeds right around a gigabyte down while indoors and a grand total of 1,109 Mbps down / 236 Mbps up when outdoors. This is not unheard-of for my area, but it is also not the norm, either. I will continue to test this throughout the review period. In terms of performance from the A20 Pro processor, VoiceOver (the built-in screen reader for blind, DeafBlind, and low vision people) is as fast and responsive as one could possibly want it to be. The moment I put my finger on the screen, VoiceOver is off and talking. That said, VoiceOver in iOS 27 already runs exceptionally well on the A19 series of chips from last year’s devices, and there’s only so much “can this be any more responsive?” before you hit an inevitable ceiling. Is VoiceOver ‘more’ responsive on the A20 Pro processor in iPhone 18 Pro than last year’s A19 Pro? Yes, but not by much—and again, this is only because VoiceOver already runs so well on last year’s A19-equipped devices to begin with. And that’s about all I can confidently speak to right now. Battery life seems good so far, though of course it’s day one and any serious testing will need to wait until after the various background tasks finish in the next couple days. Performance is good. Sound is very good. Call quality and cellular performance also seem good. I am excited for the coming weeks. Watch this space.

news.body:
La movilidad accesible continúa siendo uno de los grandes retos para las personas ciegas y con baja visión. BUDD-e es el robot guía que quiere revolucionar la movilidad accesible se presenta como una de las iniciativas de investigación más innovadoras desarrolladas en los últimos años.

Este robot guía autónomo desarrollado por el Politécnico de Milán (Italia) pretende facilitar los desplazamientos en espacios públicos estructurados como hospitales, centros deportivos, parques o centros comerciales. Se trata de un prototipo de investigación , no de un producto comercial, pero ya ha sido probado con usuarios reales y los primeros resultados muestran una buena aceptación.

BUDD-e, cuyas siglas corresponden a Blind-assistive aUtonomous Droid Device , es un proyecto multidisciplinar liderado por investigadores del Politécnico de Milán. Su objetivo es desarrollar un robot capaz de guiar de forma segura a personas con discapacidad visual mediante una interacción física sencilla e intuitiva.

A diferencia de otros sistemas de ayuda a la movilidad, BUDD-e no pretende que el usuario siga instrucciones por voz constantemente. En su lugar, utiliza un sistema de guiado físico que permite percibir de manera natural la dirección que debe seguir durante el recorrido.

Los investigadores han concebido BUDD-e para funcionar principalmente en entornos estructurados , donde la navegación puede planificarse previamente.

Entre los escenarios previstos destacan:

La idea es que, en el futuro, estos espacios puedan ofrecer el robot como un servicio. El usuario reservaría BUDD-e al llegar y el robot lo acompañaría hasta el destino seleccionado dentro de las instalaciones.

BUDD-e utiliza una plataforma robótica equipada con diversos sensores que le permiten detectar el entorno y desplazarse de forma autónoma.

Uno de sus elementos más característicos es el denominado Smart Tether System , un cable inteligente que conecta el robot con la persona usuaria.

Este sistema ejerce una ligera fuerza constante sobre la mano del usuario para indicar la dirección correcta del recorrido. Según explican sus desarrolladores, el robot no arrastra a la persona , sino que adapta continuamente su velocidad para mantener una distancia constante y acompañar el ritmo de la marcha.

Para orientarse, BUDD-e combina distintas tecnologías según el entorno:

Uno de los aspectos más relevantes del proyecto es que no se ha quedado únicamente en el laboratorio.

El robot ya ha sido evaluado con voluntarios con discapacidad visual en escenarios reales, entre ellos el Hospital Metropolitano Niguarda y el Centro Deportivo Giuriati , ambos situados en Milán.

Los investigadores publicaron recientemente los resultados de estas pruebas en la revista científica Control Engineering Practice . En el artículo describen el diseño del robot, su funcionamiento y la validación experimental realizada con usuarios reales.

Según el equipo de investigación, los ensayos muestran un buen nivel de aceptación por parte de los participantes , además de un funcionamiento satisfactorio durante las tareas de guiado.

El desarrollo de BUDD-e ha contado desde el principio con la participación de organizaciones especializadas en discapacidad visual.

Entre las entidades colaboradoras figuran:

Además, antes del diseño del robot, los investigadores realizaron cuestionarios a personas ciegas y con baja visión para conocer sus necesidades reales de movilidad.

Estos estudios mostraron que muchas personas siguen dependiendo de familiares, amistades o voluntarios para desplazarse en determinados espacios públicos, lo que motivó el desarrollo de una solución que pudiera aumentar su autonomía en esos entornos.

Por el momento, no .

Los propios investigadores presentan BUDD-e como un prototipo experimental orientado a facilitar la movilidad en determinados espacios públicos preparados para su funcionamiento.

Actualmente no existen evidencias que indiquen que pueda reemplazar al bastón blanco ni al perro guía en la movilidad cotidiana por calles o entornos urbanos complejos.

Su principal objetivo es ofrecer una ayuda adicional en lugares donde previamente se haya cartografiado el entorno y el robot pueda desplazarse de forma autónoma con seguridad.

La robótica aplicada a la accesibilidad está viviendo una rápida evolución gracias a los avances en inteligencia artificial, navegación autónoma y percepción del entorno.

BUDD-e representa una de las propuestas más avanzadas en este ámbito al combinar sensores, algoritmos de planificación y una interfaz física diseñada específicamente para personas con discapacidad visual.

Aunque todavía se encuentra en fase de investigación, el proyecto demuestra el potencial que puede tener la robótica para ampliar las opciones de movilidad accesible en espacios públicos durante los próximos años.

news.body:
PDF documents are everywhere, from reports and forms to manuals and online resources. These documents can be accessed via a web browser or application like Adobe Acrobat Reader.

When PDFs are formatted correctly, they can be read using standard navigation commands and JAWS Quick Navigation Keys; however, challenges arise when the PDF is not structured correctly. Details like headings, reading order, table structure, and labeled form fields — tell JAWS what to say and in what order. Whether that structure exists at all, and whether it matches what a sighted reader sees, is what separates an accessible PDF from an inaccessible one.

news.title: Jieshuo Touch Focus And Double Tap Delays
news.summary: Whether you are exploring the screen or trying to find a specific element, there is a delay between touching the screen and focusing on the…
news.body:
Published 16 September 2026 by Kareen Kiwan

Whether you are exploring the screen or trying to find a specific element, there is a delay between touching the screen and focusing on the element under your finger. Similar to TalkBack, Jieshuo screen reader allows you to change the value of this delay. It also allows you to set the time in which 2 taps are registered as an accessibility double tap.

In order to change the touch focus delay and double tap delay values, you must first enable handling gestures directly through Jieshuo. To do this, go to Advanced settings > Operation settings and check the Handle gestures in the screen reader checkbox.

The next item in this section is for setting the touch focus delay value. Available values are 150, 200, 250, and 300 milliseconds. To change the time for double tap registration, select Double tap delay and choose any of the available values. The same values as those available for the touch focus delay are provided here.

In the same settings section, you will find an option called One-finger system gesture trigger range, with the following ranges: small, medium, big, and maximum. This setting defines the distance the finger needs to cover when performing one-finger system navigation gestures, such as swiping up from the bottom to go to Home.

news.title: Stactiles: las pegatinas táctiles de Hable One que hacen accesible cualquier vitrocerámica
news.summary: Las superficies táctiles han cambiado la forma en la que utilizamos muchos electrodomésticos, pero también pueden convertirse en una barrera para las personas ciegas o con baja visión. Para facilitar la identificación de controles y funciones, Hable One ha desarrollado Stactiles, unas pegatinas táctiles que están ganando popularidad entre usuarios con discapacidad visual y que […] La entrada Stactiles: las pegatinas táctiles de Hable One que hacen accesible cualquier vitrocerámica se publicó primero en Conticgo .
news.body:
Las superficies táctiles han cambiado la forma en la que utilizamos muchos electrodomésticos, pero también pueden convertirse en una barrera para las personas ciegas o con baja visión. Para facilitar la identificación de controles y funciones, Hable One ha desarrollado Stactiles , unas pegatinas táctiles que están ganando popularidad entre usuarios con discapacidad visual y que pueden utilizarse, entre otros dispositivos, en cocinas y placas de vitrocerámica.

Stactiles son unas pegatinas con relieve y diferentes texturas diseñadas para proporcionar una referencia táctil sobre superficies que, de otro modo, resultan completamente lisas.

La propuesta de Hable One es sencilla: colocar una pequeña marca táctil sobre el control que se quiere identificar para poder localizarlo mediante el tacto. Las pegatinas incorporan colores de alto contraste y diferentes formas, símbolos o texturas, por lo que pueden servir tanto como referencia visual como táctil.

La compañía dispone de diferentes colecciones, entre ellas conjuntos de formas básicas, símbolos, emojis, letras y Braille.

Uno de los usos que más interés está despertando es su aplicación en los electrodomésticos de cocina .

Las placas de vitrocerámica y otros aparatos modernos utilizan cada vez más paneles de control táctiles. Al desaparecer los botones físicos, una persona con baja visión puede tener dificultades para localizar un determinado control o distinguir entre diferentes funciones.

Las Stactiles permiten colocar referencias táctiles en puntos concretos del panel. Por ejemplo, pueden utilizarse para identificar el botón de encendido, determinadas temperaturas o niveles de potencia, o establecer una referencia que facilite localizar los diferentes controles.

Hable One señala específicamente que sus Stactiles son resistentes al calor y al agua , y las recomienda para marcar controles de hornos, freidoras de aire y lavadoras, entre otros electrodomésticos.

En una vitrocerámica, por ejemplo, una persona podría establecer una referencia táctil que le permita encontrar con mayor facilidad el botón de encendido y, a partir de ahí, orientarse sobre el resto de controles.

Una de las características más interesantes de Stactiles es que no todas las pegatinas tienen el mismo relieve.

La colección de formas básicas incluye símbolos como círculos, cuadrados, triángulos, signos más y menos o chevrones, además de diferentes texturas. De esta forma, no es necesario utilizar siempre el mismo tipo de marca para todos los controles.

Esto puede permitir crear un sistema de referencias personalizado. Por ejemplo, una textura podría utilizarse para identificar el encendido, otra para los controles de aumento y disminución y otra para localizar una función concreta.

La elección y colocación de las marcas dependerá, lógicamente, de las necesidades y preferencias de cada persona.

Su utilidad no se limita a los electrodomésticos.

Hable One ha diseñado Stactiles para poder utilizarse también sobre superficies táctiles , proporcionando un punto físico de referencia sobre interfaces que normalmente no ofrecen ningún tipo de relieve.

Según la información del fabricante, el material permite presionar a través de la propia pegatina para activar el control situado debajo. Esto abre posibilidades interesantes para adaptar diferentes dispositivos electrónicos que utilizan paneles planos y táctiles.

Este planteamiento resulta especialmente interesante porque una de las tendencias actuales en diseño de electrodomésticos y dispositivos electrónicos es precisamente la sustitución de botones físicos por controles táctiles.

La principal ventaja de este tipo de productos es precisamente su sencillez.

No requieren instalar una aplicación ni modificar electrónicamente el electrodoméstico. Se trata de añadir referencias físicas a una interfaz que originalmente no las tiene .

Además, pueden combinarse con otras estrategias de accesibilidad. En una cocina, por ejemplo, una persona puede utilizar referencias táctiles junto con contraste de color, iluminación adecuada y otras técnicas de organización que faciliten la orientación.

No obstante, las Stactiles no convierten por sí solas un electrodoméstico en completamente accesible. Su utilidad dependerá del diseño del aparato, de la distribución de sus controles y de las necesidades visuales y táctiles de cada usuario.

Durante las últimas semanas, las Stactiles han comenzado a aparecer con frecuencia en publicaciones de usuarios con baja visión y ceguera en redes sociales: vídeo

Algunos usuarios están mostrando cómo las utilizan para adaptar electrodomésticos que originalmente carecen de controles físicos, como microondas, lavavajillas o aparatos de cocina.

Este tipo de demostraciones resulta especialmente interesante porque permite ver una aplicación muy práctica de la tiflotecnología: adaptar objetos cotidianos sin necesidad de sustituirlos por productos específicos para personas con discapacidad visual .

Las Stactiles son un buen ejemplo de cómo pequeñas modificaciones pueden marcar una diferencia importante en el día a día.

Frente a dispositivos tecnológicos más complejos, estas pegatinas ofrecen una solución física, económica y relativamente sencilla para introducir referencias táctiles en objetos que hasta ahora podían resultar difíciles de utilizar de forma autónoma.

En el caso de las cocinas, donde la identificación precisa de los controles es especialmente importante, disponer de referencias táctiles puede facilitar la interacción con placas, hornos y otros electrodomésticos.

La aparición de soluciones como Stactiles también pone sobre la mesa una cuestión más amplia: cuando los controles físicos desaparecen, la accesibilidad debe seguir estando presente en el diseño de las interfaces .

Mientras los fabricantes continúan apostando por superficies táctiles y controles cada vez más minimalistas, productos como estas pegatinas muestran una forma sencilla de recuperar parte de la información física que se pierde con ese cambio.
